text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes treatment involves lifestyle modifications, blood sugar monitoring, medications, and surgical options.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle modifications, blood sugar monitoring, medications, and surgical options

list.snippet: Healthy Diet: Focus on lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, complex carbohydrates, and high-fiber foods while limiting processed foods and added sugars.
Physical Activity: Aim for at least 150 minutes of aerobic and strength exercise per week to improve insulin sensitivity and lower blood sugar.
Weight Management: Losing 5% or more of body weight helps improve glycemic control.
Metformin: The standard first-line oral medication that decreases liver glucose production and increases insulin sensitivity.
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists / Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonists: Injectable (or oral) medications like semaglutide or tirzepatide that lower blood sugar, support weight loss, and protect heart health.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: Oral medications (such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin) that help the kidneys remove excess sugar through urine while benefiting heart and kidney function.
Sulfonylureas and Glinides: Oral drugs that stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
DPP-4 Inhibitors: Oral medications that help maintain higher incretin levels to lower blood sugar without causing weight gain.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Oral medications like pioglitazone that improve insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat tissue.
Insulin Therapy: Injected synthetic insulin (via pens, syringes, or pumps) used when oral and non-insulin injectable options are no longer enough.
Other Medicines: Medications to manage coexisting high blood pressure or high cholesterol.

Bariatric (Weight-Loss) Surgery: A procedure like gastric bypass or a duodenal switch that can significantly improve or even induce remission of type 2 diabetes in qualifying patients with higher BMIs.

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more detailed guidance from the Mayo Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide, review medication categories via the American Diabetes Association, or read comprehensive overviews at the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.
